title: Solid, Plastic, E-waste and Hazardous Waste

cards.b:
India generates tens of millions of tonnes of solid waste a year, and city dumps like Ghazipur in Delhi are visible failures. UPSC asks about the rule sets, the EPR idea and global treaties.

Learn each rule with its year. Mains likes the idea that waste is a resource problem, not just a disposal problem.

Reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose. Landfill is the last option. A circular economy keeps materials in use.

Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) makes the maker of a product responsible for its waste after use. It is the main tool in Indian rules for plastics, e-waste, batteries and tyres.

The 2016 rules replaced the 2000 rules. They require source segregation into wet, dry and domestic hazardous waste, extend to areas beyond municipal limits, bring in bulk waste generators, and push composting and waste-to-energy.

Revised rules were in preparation at the time of writing; check the latest status. Related: Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban) 2.0 aims at garbage-free cities. Indore is the model city.

The Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 were amended in 2021. Identified single-use plastics were banned from 1 July 2022. Carry bag thickness was raised to 75 microns (September 2021) and 120 microns (December 2022).

The 2022 EPR guidelines for plastic packaging set recycling targets and mandate registration on a central portal. Plastic credits can be traded.

India is among the largest producers of e-waste. The 2022 rules (in force April 2023) replaced the 2016 rules. They set EPR targets and certificates for producers, and cover refurbishers and recyclers.

Informal recyclers handle most e-waste, exposing workers to lead, mercury and burning fumes. Linking them to formal channels is a major Mains point.

• Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules 2016: includes control of cross-border movement.
  • Bio-Medical Waste Rules 2016 with colour-coded bags.
  • Construction and Demolition Waste Rules 2016.
  • Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 with EPR.
  • Basel Convention (1989) bans dumping of hazardous waste in poorer countries; Rotterdam (1998) is prior informed consent; Stockholm (2001) targets persistent organic pollutants.

The UN agreed in 2022 to negotiate a legally binding plastics treaty. Talks in Busan (December 2024) and Geneva (August 2025) ended without agreement, split over production caps versus waste management.

India’s stance favours waste management and common but differentiated responsibilities, and resists production caps.

EPR can fund recycling, but credits may be traded on paper without real collection. Critics say the rules ignore the role of waste pickers, who are the real recyclers.

Waste-to-energy plants also face criticism for low-calorific mixed waste, air emissions and costs. Source segregation, not technology, is the weak link.

Landfill fires and trash mountains at Ghazipur, Bhalswa and Deonar are recurring news. Programmes such as Swachh Bharat and bio-mining of legacy waste try to clear them.

Indore, Surat and Ambikapur show that segregation and community systems work. Kerala’s Haritha Karma Sena uses women’s groups.

Mains-style: “E-waste is an emerging threat. Examine India’s regulatory framework and gaps.” Structure: scale; rules (2016 then 2022 EPR); implementation gaps (informal sector, low collection); way forward (formalisation, design for repair, right to repair).

Mains-style: “Discuss EPR as a tool for plastic waste management.”

Prelims tip: Learn each year: SWM 2016, Plastic 2016 (amended 2021), E-waste 2022, Battery 2022. Basel = hazardous waste.

quiz.q: Which convention deals with hazardous waste movement?
quiz.w: Basel (1989). Stockholm is POPs; Rotterdam is PIC; Minamata is mercury.
It places post-use responsibility on producers.

quiz.q: Identified single-use plastics were banned in India from:
quiz.w: The ban took effect on 1 July 2022.

Which colour-coded system applies to the Bio-Medical Waste Rules?
quiz.w: The rules mandate four colour categories.
POPs such as DDT are covered.
